lead: IoT, the Internet of Things, is a network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little or no direct human control. The idea exists because cheap chips, wireless links and cloud services let ordinary objects report facts and receive commands. A smart water meter in a city, a home thermostat and a crop sensor in a field are common uses. This chapter fixes the definition, names the characteristics that separate IoT from a simple connected gadget, and traces how machine links, tags, sensor networks, IP, cloud platforms, edge computing and AI built today's systems.

blocks.text: IoT is a network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little or no direct human control. Three words carry the definition.

A thing is a physical object with an identity, such as a meter, lamp, lock or pump. The identity lets the network name that object and its data. The physical design of things and their parts is in 1.2.

The internet is a network of networks that moves data using Internet Protocol (IP) addresses and routing. In IoT the internet may end at a gateway; the last link to a thing can be short-range radio. Data can still travel beyond one cable or room.
A service is the useful result: a bill, a warning, a closed valve, a cooled room. A sensor alone is not IoT. The system must use the sensed data and often act on the physical world.

Little or no direct human control means rules and software run the loop. A person may set a threshold once; after that the system reports, decides and acts. This separates IoT from a person reading a meter and typing the value. Some syllabi call this definition and characteristics of IoT, foundations, or evolution. The logical functions behind the service are in 1.3.
Eight characteristics appear in most definitions. They create design trade-offs.

items: Connectivity: a thing must have a communication path, wired or wireless, to send data and receive commands.
Identity: each thing has a unique name or address, so data can be tied to the right object. A reading without identity is only a number.
Sensing: the thing measures a property of the world, such as flow, temperature, light or motion.
Actuation: the thing changes the world, such as closing a valve, switching a lamp or locking a door.
Intelligence: some processing decides what to send or do. It can be a simple threshold; it need not be machine learning.
Energy limit: many things run on batteries or harvested power. Radio and sensing use energy, so designers use sleep schedules and send summaries, not every raw sample.
Heterogeneity: devices differ in processors, radios, power and data formats. Gateways and common data models make them work together.
Dynamic operation: things join, leave, move and fail. The network and software must handle changes without a person reconfiguring every device.

blocks.text: These characteristics explain why IoT is more than a sensor with a Wi-Fi chip. Sensor and actuator details are in Unit 2; enabling technologies are in 1.6.

sections.h3: Evolution from M2M to edge AI

blocks.text: Evolution is a chain of borrowings, not one invention.
Early machine-to-machine (M2M) links connected machines directly for remote monitoring and control, often in factories and utilities. They worked without internet-scale addressing.
Radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags identified objects by radio. Supply chains and toll plazas used them, but a tag mainly carried identity, not a full sensing network.
Wireless sensor networks (WSN) put small sensing nodes into multi-hop radio networks. Battery life limited them, and they often used custom protocols.
IP and cloud changed scale. Embedded devices could use IP or reach an IP gateway, and cloud servers stored and analysed data from many sites. This is the internet-scale step.
IoT platforms made device management practical: registration, dashboards, rules, APIs and billing. A platform is the highlighted stage in the figure.

Edge and AI moved some decisions near the thing. Local processing cuts delay, saves bandwidth and can keep raw data private. Small machine-learning models can classify vibration or images on the device.
M2M versus IoT is compared in 1.7. Impact is summarised only in one line here; details are in 1.8.

examples.question: A city installs 2,000 smart water meters. Each meter sends 24 readings per day. Each reading is 40 bytes. Find the raw data per day in kB. Take 1 kB = 1000 bytes. Ignore packet headers and retransmissions.
steps: Readings per day = 2,000 meters × 24 readings per meter per day = 48,000 readings per day.
Bytes per day = 48,000 readings per day × 40 bytes per reading = 1,920,000 bytes per day.
Data in kB = 1,920,000 bytes per day ÷ 1000 bytes per kB = 1,920 kB per day.
examples.answer: The raw data is 1,920 kB per day.

traps: Do not define IoT as only internet-connected sensors. The service and the action on the physical world are part of the definition.
A sensor alone is not an IoT system. It needs identity, a communication path and a use of its data; an actuator alone is also not enough.
M2M is not a synonym for IoT. M2M often uses direct links; IoT adds internet-scale addressing, cloud services and human-facing applications.
Use 1 kB = 1000 bytes in this chapter's data examples. Mixing in 1024 changes the answer.
RFID proves identity, not necessarily sensing. A tag can say which object it is without measuring flow, temperature or light.

quiz.a: IoT is a network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little or no direct human control.
Any four of connectivity, identity, sensing, actuation, intelligence, energy limit, heterogeneity, dynamic operation.

quiz.q: Why is 'little or no direct human control' part of the definition?
quiz.a: It separates an automated sensing-and-action loop from a person reading a meter or switching a pump. Software applies rules; a human may set them once.

quiz.q: A farm has 500 soil sensors. Each sends 6 readings per hour. Each reading is 20 bytes. Find raw bytes per day.
quiz.a: Readings per day = 500 × 6 × 24 = 72,000. Bytes per day = 72,000 × 20 = 1,440,000 bytes per day.

quiz.q: A toll plaza uses passive RFID tags and readers, and automatically deducts the fee. Is this IoT? Justify with the definition.
quiz.a: Yes, if the tags identify vehicles, readers send data to a system, and the system deducts the fee with little human control. It uses identity and connectivity; sensing is limited to tag detection.

quiz.q: Distinguish sensing and actuation with one example each.
quiz.a: Sensing measures a property, such as a flow sensor counting litres. Actuation changes the world, such as a valve closing the pipe.

quiz.q: Why does the energy limit force duty cycling in a battery-powered sensor?
quiz.a: Radio transmission and continuous sensing drain a small battery. Duty cycling keeps the device asleep most of the time, wakes it to sample and send summaries, and so trades update rate for months or years of life.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now speaks of digital twins, asset tracking and predictive maintenance, which combine the same blocks with cloud analytics. Research explores batteryless sensing, TinyML on microcontrollers, and interoperable device discovery. Newer curricula connect IoT with cyber-physical systems and edge computing; search for 'TinyML', 'digital twin IoT' and 'batteryless sensor' to go further.
